Part 1

Before You Read

Chapter 1About This Source
Chapter 1

About This Source

Robert Jackson spoke on the second day of the trial, to the four judges, the defendants, and a courtroom full of reporters. The speech took most of a day. It was broadcast in part, and it was printed in newspapers around the world. The excerpt below is from its opening, before he turned to the evidence.

A few words may be new. “Malignant” means full of hatred and evil. “Flushed with victory” means excited by winning. “Vengeance” means revenge. A “poisoned chalice” is a cup of poison, and in Shakespeare’s play Macbeth the phrase warns that the evil one does returns to the doer.

Read this as a historian should. Ask who is being addressed and what Jackson wants them to feel. Ask what he says is unusual about this trial. Ask what standard he sets for himself and the other judges.

The First Trial

Chapter 2The Opening Passages, in Plain English
Chapter 3The Opening Passages, in the Original
Chapter 2

The Opening Passages, in Plain English

Plain version, written for this page. These are not Jackson's words.

The first passage says the privilege of opening the first trial in history for crimes against the peace of the world brings a grave responsibility. It says the wrongs the trial seeks to condemn and punish were so calculated, so malignant, and so devastating that civilization cannot tolerate their being ignored, because it cannot survive their being repeated.

The next passage says that four great nations, flushed with victory and stung with injury, stay the hand of vengeance and voluntarily submit their captive enemies to the judgment of the law. It calls this one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid to Reason.

Chapter 3

The Opening Passages, in the Original

The original: the opening passages. [...] marks a cut.

The privilege of opening the first trial in history for crimes against the peace of the world imposes a grave responsibility. The wrongs which we seek to condemn and punish have been so calculated, so malignant, and so devastating, that civilization cannot tolerate their being ignored, because it cannot survive their being repeated.

That four great nations, flushed with victory and stung with injury stay the hand of vengeance and voluntarily submit their captive enemies to the judgment of the law is one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid to Reason.

Chapter 4

The Last Passage, in Plain English

Plain version, written for this page. These are not Jackson's words.

The last passage says we must never forget that the record on which the court judges these defendants today is the record on which history will judge those who judge them tomorrow. It says that to pass these defendants a poisoned chalice is to put it to our own lips as well.

Chapter 5

The Last Passage, in the Original

The original: the last passage.

We must never forget that the record on which we judge these defendants today is the record on which history will judge us tomorrow. To pass these defendants a poisoned chalice is to put it to our own lips as well.

Chapter 6

A Note for You

From the page

Notice that Jackson says the winners could have taken vengeance and chose not to. Ask what reason he gives for the difference between vengeance and a trial. Notice also the last sentence, and ask who is being warned. You can return to this page as often as you like.
